newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's Walesa says may start new party after vote.
newsitem.headline: Poland's Walesa says may start new party after vote.

text.p: Lech Walesa, Poland's former president and first leader of the Solidarity union, said on Thursday he would form a new party to challenge ex-communists if they won this year's parliamentary elections.

Walesa, who has kept a low profile since his narrow defeat by ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski in presidential polls in late 1995, said he wanted to give the fragile Solidarity-led rightist coalition time to consolidate.
"Until the elections I won't be destabilising those fragile political ties," Walesa told Reuters in an interview.
"Right now there is no room for Lech Walesa because I'm a patriot and I don't want to take anyone's electorates...but after the polls I will have to go back to politics."
He said that if the Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS) grouping some 30 small rightist parties emerged victorious, he would limit his political role to an advising, supporting and controlling one.
"But if...there is a ex-communist victory then I will have to unleash a lightning force that will shatter the commies," he said.
He said he would build a new-style party capable of ousting the now-ruling left in the next parliamentary elections but said it was still too early to give any details.

Walesa, who before the 1993 parliamentary polls predicted the victory of parties rooted in the communist era -- the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and the Polish Peasant Party (PSL) -- would not give his prediction for this year's elections.
"Then it (the prediction) served as a wake-up call for the fragmented right, now I could spoil something," he said.
Walesa said he was adamant about ousting ex-communists because he believed they grouped opportunists who shared little in terms of values and lacked credibility as a political force.

"Perhaps I'm doing them injustice but I suspect that what keeps them together is fear of being held accountable for the past and craving for power...they are well educated...but they lack common values," he said.
"So I don't know who I am dealing with, who is ruling the country," he said.
Walesa also criticised the new constitution, passed by the National Assembly on Wednesday, for failing to strengthen presidential powers.
"I wanted a constitution that would give power to the president ... Poland squeezed between Germany and Russia and with difficult reforms on its hands needs a powerful executive," he said.

Commenting on the recent summit between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian leader Boris Yeltsin, and on Poland's chances of winning fast NATO entry, Walesa said he was disappointed with the tone of recent discussions on NATO enlargement.

"This is not what I was waiting for although we don't have anything in writing yet. My vision is: let's keep expanding one pact so there will be no material to build a second one. It is a peaceful concept which doesn't entail any arms upgrade."

Walesa said that if such thinking prevailed, Poland's curse of geographical location between Russia and Germany could be turned into an economic blessing allowing the country fully to benefit from its central location.
